cues.text: Chapter eight.
The AgriTech Solutions case.
Let us now work through a case study, because a case lets us see how the ideas of digital transformation behave when they meet real constraints.
Before we begin, one important point: this is an educational case.
It is a teaching example, not an independently audited report, and we will keep that distinction in mind as we go.
The case describes a Nigerian agriculture platform called FarmConnect.
What does FarmConnect do?
It connects four groups of people: farmers, experts, suppliers and buyers.
Think of it as a digital meeting place.
A farmer might need advice from an agronomy expert, seeds or fertiliser from a supplier, and a buyer for the harvest.
FarmConnect brings all of these parties onto one platform, so that information, products and money can move between them.
Now, here is where the trouble began.
The platform relied on central infrastructure.
In plain terms, that means one main set of computing resources handled the work for everybody.
When few people are using it, that can be fine.
But agriculture is seasonal.
At planting time and at harvest, huge numbers of users arrive at once.
These are the peak seasons.
During those periods, the central infrastructure became a bottleneck.
A bottleneck is like the narrow neck of a bottle: no matter how much is waiting to pour, everything must squeeze through one small opening, and so everything slows down.
The case names four consequences.
First, delays.
Pages loaded slowly and requests waited.
Second, missed market opportunities.
In farming, timing matters enormously.
If a farmer cannot reach a buyer or a price quickly, the chance may pass, and produce can lose value.
Third, rural connectivity problems.
Many farmers live where mobile networks are weak or unreliable, so even a fast platform may be hard to reach.
Fourth, internal resistance.
Some people inside the organisation resisted change.
This is a classic organisational challenge, and it reminds us that technology problems are rarely only technology problems.
Notice that two of these four are technical, and two are human and contextual.
Next, the response.
The case describes a combined response, and the word combined is important, because no single fix was used.
Let us take the components in order.
The first component is scalable cloud and distributed infrastructure.
Instead of one central system, the work is spread across many computing resources, and capacity can grow when demand rises and shrink when it falls.
Scalable means it can stretch to meet a peak.
Distributed means the load is shared rather than carried by one point.
This directly targets the bottleneck.
The second component is stakeholder engagement based on Kotter.

This refers to John Kotter's approach to leading change, which emphasises building urgency, bringing together a guiding group of supporters, communicating a vision, and involving people so that they help carry the change rather than resist it.
Here it addresses the internal resistance.
The source tells us the engagement was Kotter-based, and we will not add detail beyond that.
The third component is a mobile-first experience.
Mobile-first means the service is designed first for the smartphone, and then adapted for other devices.
This matters because for many farmers the phone is the main, and sometimes only, way to get online.
The fourth component is CRM and chatbots.
CRM stands for customer relationship management.
It is a way of recording and managing interactions with users, so that the organisation understands their needs and history.
Chatbots are automated conversational tools that can answer common questions at any hour, without a person on every line.
The fifth component is predictive crop advice.
This uses data and analytical models to anticipate what is likely to happen, and so to suggest what a farmer might do.
It is a good example of data-driven decisions supporting a real agricultural choice.
Now consider training and user needs.
Training included webinars, which are online sessions, and rural on-site workshops, which are in-person sessions held where the farmers actually are.
Why both?
Because webinars reach people at scale, but they depend on connectivity, while on-site workshops reach those the network does not.

To meet user needs, the platform used simplified interfaces, meaning fewer and clearer screens and options, and multilingual support, so that farmers could use the service in languages they are comfortable with.
Finally, surveys and feedback guided ongoing improvements.
This makes the transformation a continuing cycle of listening and adjusting, rather than a one-time project.
Now to the results.
The case reports the following.
Ninety-nine point nine percent uptime, meaning the platform was available almost all of the time.
It handled fifty percent more users during peaks.
Response times improved by forty percent.
Satisfaction scores improved by twenty-five percent.
Farmer adoption exceeded eighty percent within six months.
And costs fell by fifteen percent.
Now, a careful learner does not simply accept these numbers.
The source is explicit: these are teaching case claims, not independent measurements.
So how should we evaluate them?
Four questions are suggested.
First, baselines: forty percent better than what?
Without knowing the starting point, a percentage tells us little.
Second, sampling: who was surveyed, and how many?
A satisfaction score from only the easiest-to-reach users could mislead.
Third, rural inclusion: did the measured users include the rural farmers who faced the connectivity problems, or mainly those already well connected?
Fourth, sustainability: were the improvements sustained over time, or only a short-term gain after launch?
The case closes with a vital lesson.
Cloud alone would not resolve literacy, training or process problems.
Better servers cannot teach someone to use an application, and they cannot fix a poorly designed workflow.
That is why the response paired infrastructure with training, simplified design, language support and change management.
Digital transformation succeeds when technology, people and processes are changed together.
